en: This text employs two systems of enumeration. At times, the material is organized into twelve thematic sections and numbered accordingly;
these numbers are provided in brackets. The editions consulted were as follows:
— *Stava-kalpa-druma*, edited by Bhakti Saranga Goswami. Vrndavana, 1959.
— *Śrī-śrī-caitanya-candrāmṛta*, edited by...
*Bhakti Vilāsa Tīrtha*. Mayapur, Chaitanya Math. Third edition, 1992.
Texts without an alternative number are not found in either one of [the two].

Regarding the various editions, no attempt has been made to provide alternative readings. We praise that Lord of the Youth of Vraja, whose form is pure consciousness, who possesses boundless and supremely wonderful magnanimity, in order to savor his excellence.
To bestow upon others the waves of the sweet nectar of the intoxication of pure self-love, and to reveal the New Island of the Supreme Abode;
(1) whose true nature cannot be perceived even by all the crest-jewels of the Vedas.
He who possesses some uniquely sweet and beautiful path that is inaccessible even to Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods,
and by whom this entire world was suddenly made intoxicated with the wine of the nectar of Lord Hari—
he, the glorious Moon of Caitanya, how could he possibly be within the range of my words or my mind? (2) (137)
Established in the Dharma with incomparable steadfastness, bearing the most exalted devotion to Viṣṇu, and possessing a heart that is, alas, as hard as stone, this base man—
worse even than a cow-killer— now floods the world with torrents of tears!
Who indeed knows this most profound stage, where the golden-hued limbs are the very color of gold?

(3) One who is untouched by dharma, yet constantly possessed by the supreme, has attained a vision toward extreme unrighteousness; he is certainly not present anywhere among the creations of the virtuous.
I praise that certain Lord who, intoxicated by the taste of the nectar of the divine Hari’s rasa bestowed upon him, dances wildly, sings aloud, and rolls about on the ground;
(4) from whom the wave of the Blessed One's name suddenly emerges. (2)

Alas, even though these embodied beings were surrounded by many sins, their hearts—even those as hard as adamant—became like fresh butter; that fair-complexioned Lord who descends into such a world is my refuge. (5) (110)
There is no yoga, no meditation, nor chanting, austerity, renunciation, or observances;
there are no Vedas, nor right conduct, nor indeed any cessation from forbidden acts— yet, alas,
all this suddenly descends upon consciousness in one whose heart has compassion as its essence.
In this world, people joyfully plunder that supreme crest-jewel among the goals of human life,

which has not been attained by those devoted to ritual action (*karma*), nor reached through austerity, meditation, and yoga; nor even conceived by anyone through dispassion, renunciation, the principles of truth, praises, or logic.

I bow to that fair-complexioned One, whose secret even those who possess love for Govinda have not grasped; He who manifests Himself by His own name alone, wherein the Supreme descends. (3) Fie upon those of dull intellect who speak of themselves as "I am Brahmā," their faces blooming with pride!
Fie, fie upon those attached to ritual acts, and fie upon those who perform harsh penances and those who practice self-restraint!
Why do we lament these human-beasts intoxicated by the flavors of sense-objects?
Alas, not even a trace of the white honey has mingled with them. (8) (32)
Tying knots with his waist-cord while his hands trembled under the weight of love,
chanting the names "Hare Kṛṣṇa" to count them for the welfare of his own people,
his face bathed in tears, he indeed went forth desiring to see the Lord of the Universe Himself.
May Hari, whose fair body brings delight to the eyes of those who have gone [to him], protect you!
(9) (16) A stone, even if saturated with the essence of nectar, can never produce a sprout;
and the tail of the Lord of Dogs (Śiva), when displayed, can never possess straightness.
O wise ones, raising your hands, how can you say "Alas, how is the orb of the moon to be sustained"?
Let everything be a means [for its attainment]; for without the radiance of white compassion, there is no festival of existence.
(10) In beauty, she is ten million Cupids; in gladdening all people, she is ten million moons.

May that fair-complexioned Lord be victorious—he who is the pinnacle of maternal affection, the pinnacle of wondrous generosity even as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, the pinnacle of profundity like the ocean, and the pinnacle of sweetness like a jewel, nectar, milk, and honey-wine; he who has displayed millions of wonders at the station of the essence of love. (11) (101)

To whom has the wondrous subject known as *prema* not reached the path of their hearing? Who is a knower of the majesty of the names [of the Lord]? Who has entered the great sweetnesses of the forests of Vṛndāvana?
Or who knows Rādhā, the ultimate limit of the sweetness of the wonder of supreme rasa?
The singular Moon of Consciousness, out of supreme compassion, has revealed everything.
(12) (130) Salutations to the Moon of Consciousness, whose splendor is like the radiance of ten million moons;
to the Moon of the ocean of the bliss of love, who smiles with the lovely rays of the moon. (13) (8)

To him, whose supreme goal of human existence— known as liberation— is attainable through devotion to his lotus feet, and who is the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious in the world; to him [I offer salutation].
Salutations again and again to Caitanya-candra!
(14) [I bow] to him who holds his two lotus-hands joined like buds above his head,
and whose pair of soft cheeks are bathed by the flowing tears from his eyes.
Bow down to the supreme light, fair as the hue of fresh lotus filaments, stealing the splendor of molten gold, draped in a *dukūla* garment;
possessing lion-like shoulders, exceedingly sweet, with the regions of his cheeks smiling. (15) (81)

May the body of Mādhava, united with Rādhā— a form consisting of wondrous and manifold transformations of an intensely radiant essence, difficult to discern, and possessing a loveliness as delightful as the interior of a full-blown golden lotus— protect you all. 16 (13)

He whose fair-complexioned splendor, shimmering with millions of waves from the ocean of the nectar of the rasa of perfect love, covers the entire universe; he who is praised by Īśvara, Brahmā, Vyāsa, and others;
and who reveals to the world his enchanting form, which is difficult to perceive even for millions of Vedas.
A marvel! On the shore of the salt ocean, the Supreme Brahman himself dances.
He is delightful with multitudes of unrestrained ropes and snares;
he is the delight of Māra’s groves, and his name is incessantly invoked.

We meditate upon the abode of compassion, the supreme abode named Caitanya, whose fair complexion shines like gold. (18) When the moon-like Gaura has descended and the ocean of love has expanded, [may we attain that state]. (69)
Even one who is utterly wretched remains truly wretched when the flood of jewels is so brilliantly revealed.
(19) (34) If anyone should accomplish the supreme goal of human life through devotion to Murāri— by means of hearing, reflecting, chanting, and so forth— it would be auspicious indeed.

But for me, there is a certain secret essence of nectar—the fair-complexioned abode of the ocean of supreme transcendental love—which is worthy of worship. Whatever series of worldly or Vedic activities has reached its ultimate conclusion [finds its fulfillment there]. (20) (58)

Or that shame felt during jesting, singing, dancing, and festivals; or those innate [virtues]—life, body, wealth, and dharma—that once existed; and even my whiteness! A certain thief of fierce prowess has stolen it all from me. (21) (60)
Even when fallen into the great stream of karma, it attains stability;
it reaches a state of fluidity harder than even great boulders;
and it dances upward, without means, by the minds of great yogis.

When the glorious Caitanya, a marvel of manifold splendor, descended upon the earth, the sensualists abandoned talk of women, sons, and the like; the wise abandoned their recitations of the scriptures;
the lords of yogis abandoned the hardships born of breath-control; and the ascetics abandoned their austerities. (22) (112)
When Caitanyacandra manifested the supreme path of bhakti-yoga, the ascetics abandoned the practice of jñāna; indeed, there was no other flavor [of spiritual experience] whatsoever.
On this circle of the earth where even the lords of sages had previously wandered in delusion, [he now shone]. //23 (113)//
The intellect of no one has ever entered that path which neither the Vedas nor Śuka knew;
yet, out of compassion, Śauri has revealed it even to his own kin.
Upon that radiant path of devotion, the beloveds of Gaura sport with ease. (24) (18)
Let those who hope for the four goals of human life worship the Lord, and let them become His servants by performing the service of Hari;
as for me, my mind is enticed by the desire for some secret word.

I take refuge at the feet of Caitanya-candra. (25) (59) My mind considers one who possesses immeasurable great merit, who has no other shelter than Hari, yet has not worshiped Caitanya, to be truly unfortunate. (26) (31)
O brother, chant the names of the Lord of Gokula, that exalted series of names;
or else meditate upon His divine, sweet form which enchants the entire world.
Alas, even the hope for liberation may arise for you at the feet blazing with the great nectar of divine love.
If the glance of mercy from Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu does not fall upon you,
then whether past, future, or present, no one— no matter who they may be— possesses any connection whatsoever to the nectar of the Lord’s lotus feet in this entire world-system. (82) 27.

Those free from envy understand all of that as the manifestation of the grace of Gaura alone, who sports by means of His supreme sovereignty in the form of His own devotion. (28) Having repeatedly relished the abundance of sweetness of His own series of names...

Having become utterly helpless with every intoxicating draught, his limbs relaxed, he was seen repeatedly crying out, "Sing! Sing the virtues of the Lord of Vraja! For those by whom this fair-complexioned youth has not been seen even once, devotion is difficult to achieve. (29) (38)
In every house there arose the tumultuous sound of the chanting of Hari’s names;
in every body there appeared a profusion of horripilation and tears;
and in every affection, the state of supreme sweetness reached its highest pinnacle.
Even from the most distant tradition, [the truth] descends into the world as "cow" (gau).
(114) In some cases there is dullness regarding ritual acts; in some cases there is chanting, austerity, yoga, and so forth;
in some cases there is the practice of worshipping Govinda; and in some cases there is pride in one's knowledge.
Alas, O Caitanya! Where have you gone? Your path is not seen anywhere; for even if the glorious devotion to Hari is radiant in some places, it remains merely as words.
Without a seed, how can there be the production of a sprout? Even a blind man cannot do so. //31 (138)//
How could a lame man climb a mountain peak?

Even if Śrī Caitanya, whose wondrous majesty consists of the nectar of Hari, were somehow to experience the impetuous force of supreme love, how could that ever happen for those who are not devotees? (32) (39)
Suddenly, this entire world was inundated on all sides by some indescribable forest of nectar from the great ocean of love;
and suddenly, it became filled with transformations never before seen or heard.
A wonder descends upon Kṛṣṇa, whose limbs possess the luster of gold.
(33) O fools! Discern the hidden path of devotion to Hari, which has never before been perceived even by the most eminent sages through their far-reaching vision.
If there is no confidence in the mind, and if that [state] seems difficult to attain, then renouncing everything without exception, go for refuge to the feet of Gaurīśvara.
(34) Only then will the discourse on Brahman and the path to liberation become sweet. (80)

The stability of worldly and Vedic order does not fall into disorder as long as those who know the scriptures do not engage in mutual dispute regarding various heterodox paths; nor does this occur so long as the devotees of the lotus feet of Śrī Caitanya have not come within the range of vision. (35) (19)
Upon the peak of the Blue Mountain in Raṅga,
the pair of bee-like eyes of Hari’s shining lotus-face always play amidst the waves of the intoxicating nectar of intense love for the deer-eyed women.
May my mind remember the bodiless, fair-limbed One who is free from all attachment.
(36) In one place, through absorption in Kṛṣṇa, it dances, performing many graceful gestures; in another, possessed by Rādhā, it cries out in piteous lamentation, "O Hari! Hari! Hari!"
In one place crawling like a child, and in another acting like a cowherd boy, Gaura, with his many-fold sweetness, causes the world to marvel.
(37) Ah! Do not act rashly; everyone laughs at your every effort.
People all around are intoxicated, tasting the nectar of the mellows of Hari;
however, listen quietly to this: the object of our love being presented here is that very same Supreme Lord who is celebrated in the Vedas—He is indeed the Fair One. 38. (83)

Some, filled with irrepressible pride on all sides and possessing minds that consider themselves blessed, master the entirety of the scriptures while remaining engaged in various high and low rituals, austerities, and the like;
yet others of perverse intent mutter only two or three names of Hari.
Formerly, and even now that the moon Gauracandra has risen, love [for Him] is common to all.
(39) Even one who is most sinful, of low birth, of evil character, the limit of wicked deeds, the lowest of outcastes, and constantly filled with impure latent impressions;

We praise only that Gaura, by whose grace one is truly uplifted— even if born in a wretched land, even if residing there, even if ruined through evil association. (40) If this entire universe were insentient and the Lord were sentience itself...
Even those who know all the scriptures do not understand; indeed, such people wander in delusion.

(41) When the Lord, whose lotus feet are sought after by the gods, descends under the name Caitanya and spreads waves of the most sweet nectar of love directed toward all beings, [even the learned are bewildered].
Who is a child? Who is an elder? Who here is dull-witted? Who is wise? Who is a wretch?

Among all those who partake in devotion at the feet of Hari, there arose an indescribable uniformity. (42) Then, having bestowed some grace and addressed them with a face radiant with the beauty of a smile—
Beholding them from afar with affectionate glances, He bestows a festival of great love;

yet alas, even toward Him, those whose intellects are hardened by fallacious reasoning show no great regard—even toward Hari, who has directly descended as the embodiment of perfect rasa. These people are simply wicked. 43 (45)
I do not even count those dwelling in Kāśī; why should I seek Gayā?
If liberation becomes as common as a pearl-oyster for me, what occasion is there for concern for others? Even in the Mahāraurava hell, no semblance of terror arises—where then could fear be found?
If that fair-complexioned God of gods feels compassion for [his] wife, sons, and others,

he manifests in the world as one who instills the essence of the primordial sweetness of the salt ocean at its shore— a sweetness throbbing with playful grace, which is the very treasury of the rasa of the young cowherd girls.
Even in her childhood play, a certain form of hers—deluding the entire universe with its own radiance and appearing as if composed of molten gold—delights my heart.
(45) Upon seeing a mass of fresh clouds, she becomes intoxicated; upon beholding a peacock feather, she becomes enraptured.
Seeing the curved garland of *guñjā* berries, he trembles, utterly overwhelmed;
even upon seeing a dark youth, he is startled and filled with wonder—may Hari, who possesses a fair body and thus displays his own love, protect you! 46. (14)
For one who is intensely fettered by the shackles and chains of endless, terrible, and evil latent tendencies, being devoted to millions of wicked deeds,
and whose mind is afflicted and tormented by millions of wrong thoughts.
Without Gaurīśa, who will be my kinsman here today?
Alas! How can the sprout of the creeper of true devotion grow upon the utterly barren soil of my mind? //47(51)//

In the heart, there is only one supreme treasure to be cherished, namely that which is called consciousness; by possessing this, one is never to be pitied. (48) [He is] an ocean of mercy, wearing a variegated garment as beautiful as the glow of the twilight sun.

May the glorious Lord of the Arts, blazing with the great, stainless light consisting of the nectar of perfect love, born from the ocean of milk that is Śacī’s womb, and possessing noble and wondrous arts, arise within the sky of my heart. 49. (15)
Where, indeed, is detachment, and where is talk of sense objects? Where is that agitation as if in hells, and where is that wave of sweetness from the weight of discipline?
Where is that extraordinary splendor, or else the path of great devotion?
Where could she possibly be found, given what has been perceived among those of fair gait—
she who is the means for the great waves of devotion to her own lotus feet, and who inspires even the greatest wonder in Śiva, Brahmā, and the others? (50) (20)
May the Lord Gaura, whose greatness is manifest as a supreme marvel, be victorious— he who, like one intoxicated, performs indescribable dances due to the onset of great divine love.
(51) All, including Nārada, Śaṅkara, and others, have arrived here, as has Śrī herself.
Even Lord Balarāma arrived and met him, and the Vṛṣṇis appeared;
furthermore, even the residents of Vraja—the cowherds, cowherdesses, and others—became manifest when Śrī Gauracandra, the sovereign of the nectar of perfect love, descended upon the earth. (52) (118)
Then all his affectionate servants, possessing exceedingly sweet, radiant, and noble qualities, descended into the presence of His two lotus feet;
they attained the splendor of the nectar of a great love even more abundant than before.
He bestows his own wonderful love upon the golden-hued world;

for he does not [bestow it] upon these attendants of Śrī Govinda, nor upon their ministers, nor upon their deeds, because of the manifestation of the playful splendor of the intoxicating essence of his extraordinary love. (53) (119)

It is a great wonder that even when the giver is present before one's eyes, the mind does not firmly fix upon Him; he who fails to recognize the Supreme Lord manifest here is a fool, a mere beast among men. (54) (40) Innumerable incarnations of the Blessed One are proclaimed in the Vedas and other scriptures.
Who could possibly conceive of a power greater than that of the Supreme Lord?
What else is there to say regarding my dearest one, for how many such experiences do the virtuous not possess?
Nevertheless, O Śrī Gaura, Hari, Hari! How many fools are there who do not perceive you as the Lord? 55 (41)
How small is this destruction of the race of Rākṣasas and Daityas; how small is this manifestation of the path of yoga and other spiritual disciplines; how small is this creation and so forth;
and how small is this lifting up of the earth—compared to the greatness of that which is radiant with love!
We praise the supreme form of the Lord Caitanya, who creates the path of devotion;

whose playful sidelong glance bestows upon all embodied beings the bliss of love, demonstrating the worthlessness of various transformations such as liberation and other goals through direct experience. //56(7)//

If the Lord Gauracandra were not hidden within the Vedas and present in this world, then the doctrine of non-divinity would prevail; O Śiva, O Śiva! Salutations to You, O Viṣṇu, whose māyā is profound.
(42) May my dwelling be in the cage of the rows of serpents that are the terrible fires.

May I never have association anywhere with those who are averse to the lotus feet of Śrī Caitanya; for even if the abode of Vaikuṇṭha and other realms were to present themselves before me, my mind would not desire them if it does not savor even a slight drop of the nectar from the lotus feet of the Fair One. (58) (65)
Once his beautiful face— timid with affection and its lotus-like eyes clouded by streams of tears brought before his sight for a single moment— has been beheld,
he never again desires to abandon the feet of the Supreme Lord.
Intoxicated by ever-new passion, he [experienced] an ocean of surging sweetness.
(59) Having practiced the Dharma, having served Viṣṇu, having wandered through sacred fords, and having reflected upon the Vedas;
Without service at the feet of Gaurī’s beloved, they do not know that station which is difficult to attain even through the Vedas and other means;
[they lack] a taste for the path of knowledge and the like, and [possess] devotion to the Lord of Vraja. //60(22)//
I do not know the proper way, nor do I meet with true gurus;
alas, alas, alas! Who shall be my refuge?
Hari, who is intensely fair, has not yet entered the path of your ears. (84)
O Lord of inconceivable majesty, even for me, a base person, that path of wondrous devotion— attained by Śiva, the parrot, Uddhava, Nārada, and others— is not far off.
O Caitanyacandra, if you cast upon us even a single glance of compassion,
then let our vain attachment to ritual actions be removed, and let not even a whisper of such talk ever reach the vicinity of our ears; let us instead follow the path of spiritual realization.
Do not direct your delusion toward the body and such; through the grace of Gaurī, the crown jewel of all human goals—exceedingly wonderful and sweet—meets you.
(63) Enough with the study of scriptures! Alas, enough with wandering to sacred pilgrimage sites!

O you who consider yourselves as mere blades of grass, fie upon you! You falsely tremble before the tigress that is woman and spit upon her; yet you, blessed ones, take refuge in the disguise of a renunciant, dancing on the shore of the ocean out of intoxication with your own aesthetic flavor. 64. (86)
Beating his hands and feet loudly, raising his arms— which were like magnificent golden staffs— and with a body trembling in a sublime *tāṇḍava* dance, he [Krishna] is seen with wide-lotus eyes,
uttering some indistinct "Hari, Hari" with cries of intoxicated joy that destroy the misfortunes of the world.
I bow to that crest-jewel of the gods, the moon of consciousness permeated with incomparable aesthetic rapture.
(65) Making the faces of the ten directions resound with *huṃ* syllables, and making the sky radiant with clusters of blossoming *kunda* and water-lilies through the waves of his boisterous laughter;

With every limb trembling like leaves shaken by the wind, Hari—fair-complexioned and moving with a gait drenched in the intoxication of the essence of love—shines forth. (66) Where is that unrestrained compassion? Where is that wondrous majesty?
O Śauri, where is that affection of yours, such as that which you have toward a cow? (56) To him whose form consists of bliss and play,
who is beautiful with a divine luster like the color of gold;
Salutations, repeated salutations to You, Caitanyacandra, the bestower of the essence of great divine love.
(68) [To You] who are the very Self of the gods, sages, and lords who consider themselves great beings...

Ah! What great surge of fortune has brought here within the range of vision the son of Śacī—the crest-jewel of the circle of the Vedas—who, though unknown by his lotus feet, effects the complete eradication of whatever pride there may be? (69) (29)

Let alone the great clamor of "great, great" throughout the entire circle of the earth or in the world; let great and wondrous supernatural power indeed be manifest! And let one surely attain the state of a beautiful four-armed being by propitiating the Lord of the Universe.
My mind holds this in high regard, for indeed, nothing is dear to it except for devotion to Śrī Gaura.

(70) He is faultless, performing beautiful dances, having shaken off all impurity and crookedness; at times, he rains down the nectar of great love that removes the threefold suffering of all living beings without exception.

A certain moon-like fair-complexioned one has appeared, radiant with the rising of fortune from the milky ocean of Śacī’s womb; his beautiful feet are tasted by the cakora-birds that are the hearts of devotees. (71) The gods sounded the celestial drums, and the chief Gandharvas sang.

The Siddhas covered this earth with continuous showers of flowers, and throngs of great ṛṣis, intent on divine hymns of praise, attended with joy Śrī Gauracandra as he performed his *tāṇḍava* dance upon the earth, intoxicated by his own love. 72. (133)
Possessing the prowess of an intoxicated young lion,
making an effort to flood the world with an ocean of love,
he is some divine, fresh golden kandalī plant.
Victorious is the gentle, fair moon!
(73) (100) An ornament upon his body [is formed] by drops of water trickling from the lotus-eyes, as beautiful as excellent pearls.
I take refuge in that fair-complexioned Hari, whose garments glow with a ruddy luster, and who possesses supreme beauty even as his hair stands on end;
he is more beautiful than Kandarpa and, oh, more purifying than the full flow of the celestial river! (74) (71)
Colder even than the moon, sweeter even than the essence of honey-wine,
greater than the wish-fulfilling tree, and more affectionate in love than a mother— when will the fair-complexioned Hari place His feet upon my heart as I meditate upon Him? (75) (72)
Having repeatedly bestowed heap after heap of the most sweet nectar of love, that one God of vast compassion, delighting this entire universe,
wears beautiful madder-dyed garments clinging to his hips.
My beloved is indeed like the tip of a fresh lightning flash, though it be merely a sound;
whether seen, touched, praised, or remembered, or even by those far away—whether bowed down to or not looked upon. (76) (73)
I bow to the compassionate Lord Śrī Caitanya, the one who alone is capable of bestowing the very essence of love.
(4) Constantly drenching the surface of his pale cheeks with the water of his eyes, he—
Exhaling again and again at every moment a long succession of sighs, crying out loudly with a most piteous sound of "Alas!
Alas!"—a certain fair-complexioned youth shines forth, submerged in the state of one separated from Vraja. (78) (108)
Alas, what is the use of fruitless paths such as yoga and the like, which are so difficult to traverse? Oh, rather,
offer devotion to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, who plunders all goals for one who practices it—
provided there exists that wondrous festival of love and hope which is unattainable even for Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods.
Then, let one take delight in that abode of Gaurī, which is sublime with its unfathomable majesty!
(79) Alas! Even the noble wives of good families laugh aloud again and again;
even those fashioned from the stones of wicked sense-objects undergo a state of complete melting. (87)
Even the ignorant on this earth despise the assembly of those who know all the scriptures when Śrī Caitanya, the essence of wondrous majesty, descends.
Generally, even before his appearance, this [despising] did not exist among those who possess complete knowledge. //80(120)//
Even in the *Sarvārthasāra*, Kṣemarāja found no footing, for his intellectual faculties were blunted;

yet, whose entry into the sweet love of devotion—resplendent with profound and noble sentiments—did he not achieve now that the moon-like Gaura has descended upon the world out of compassion? (81) (121)
Where Hari appeared, radiant as molten gold,
by his very majesty the world became immersed in the essence of love; there arose a loud and ever-increasing rite of the tumultuous chanting of Hari’s names.
Alas, does that sweet season ever return again? (82) (139) This very same blessed city of Gauḍa stands upon the earth; this is the very same shore of the ocean;
here is this glorious Puruṣottama, the Lord of Madhu; and those very same names remain.
Alas, Hari! Such a festival of love is not seen anywhere else;
O Caitanya, treasure-house of mercy, why then do you display this further majesty?
(83) This [manifestation] is like a shoreless ocean of truth, exceedingly vast.
Even if one were to obtain some incomparable, supreme essence by churning [the ocean of scriptures],
nevertheless, for those touched by the radiance of the feet of Madana-Gopāla in the form of Śrī Gaura, it possesses only a most formidable pungency. (84) (23)
Lower than even a blade of grass, with a naturally gentle and innocent appearance,
speaking words as sweet as nectar, recoiling at the mere scent of worldly objects, overwhelmed by love for Hari, and possessing an indescribable, steady composure.
It is said that these six qualities indeed belong to those who possess fair complexions in this world.
(85) O Śauri, when shall I become one whose disposition is made sincere toward Your fair body— which bestows the essence of supreme love and is my sole life-breath?

Or when, through an extraordinary and true inference regarding him, did the jewel-like light of Śrī Rādhā’s toe-nails suddenly arise within my heart? (86) [When] the earth before me was made muddy by the various torrents of my flowing tears...

Placing his cheek, pale as a jujube fruit, upon the palm of his hand, Hari himself— marveling at dwelling on the shore of the salt ocean while wearing a crimson garment and having become fair-complexioned— extends his affection for the lotus-feet of Rādhā. (87) (135)

Who is this god, with a body as fair as the interior of a golden plantain tree, showering something indescribable from the corners of his eyes— eyes moist with affection— as if pouring forth ten million oceans of the nectar of love, that fresh rasa resplendent with intense bliss?
In whatever measure one who has accumulated a mass of merit may find devotion for the fair lotus-feet of Gaurī, her mind suddenly makes it firmly rooted in its own true state. //88(61)//
In that very way, the moon-like mass of nectar from Rādhā’s lotus feet suddenly rises within the heart.
Who is this, with a waist adorned by a girdle, holding a bracelet in her hand? (89) (88)
Wearing a necklace upon his chest, earrings on his ears, and anklets on his feet,

with a crest-jewel formed by a cluster of full-blown jasmine flowers bound within the mass of his hair tied upward, the preeminent fair-skinned gallant sports while dancing, calling out his own names. (90) (132)
For one who has fallen into the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra, being swallowed by the crocodiles and sea-monsters of desire, anger, and the like;
who is fettered by evil tendencies and left without refuge.
O Caitanyacandra, grant me the support of Your feet!

(91) By Your splendor, You surpass millions upon millions of Kamadevas; by the radiance of Your glorious moon-like face, You cause the beauty of millions upon millions of blooming autumnal moons to appear dim.

Indeed, manifesting in his vastness a wish-granting tree multiplied by millions upon millions of times, my fair-complexioned Lord, through the good fortune of millions upon millions of births, shall set foot within my heart. (92) For a moment he laughs, then for a moment he weeps, and then for a moment he faints.
At one moment He rolls about, at another He runs, and then at another moment He dances;
at one moment He sighs, and at another He utters a noble cry of "Hā hā!"—thus does Gaurī-Hari sport here with the playfulness of great passion. 93. (134)
Alas! At one moment he is emaciated, at another he is stout; at one moment he is tearful, and then at another he is smiling. At one moment he is cold, and at another he is scorched by fire;
at one moment he is running, at another he is paralyzed, and at another he is talking incessantly. Oh! how strange!
May my fair body, for a moment, become mute for the sake of the Blessed One.

(94) Liberation acts like a hell; the assembly of the thirty-three gods acts like a flower in the sky; and the swarm of black cobras that are the unsubdued senses acts as if its fangs have been torn out.
We praise only that Gaura, by the majesty of whose compassionate side-glances the entire universe becomes full bliss, while even Brahmā, Mahendra, and the other gods become like mere insects.
(95) [With streams of tears from their eyes, as if they were millions of fresh rain-clouds...]

I bow to that Hari, who, under the guise of renunciation (*sannyāsa*), bears a smile of supreme bliss worthy of love, and who, through the radiance of his body, pours forth millions of oceans of nectar-like sweetness— alas! [96] (12)
The Lord, by whose own splendor the entire universe is permeated with the great aesthetic relish of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet,
who is the hidden abode of all the Vedas— him [I worship].
O you of dull mind, accept the fair-limbed Lord Caitanya—
He who is full of mercy, supremely magnanimous, whose heart has entered into all beings through manifold forms of love, and who is the abode of wonders! (57) 97.

"O fair-limbed one! O ocean of virtues! O embodiment of aesthetic rasa! O you who are dear by your own name!"—may this birth of mine pass away as I speak these words incessantly. (98) [Those] intoxicated by drinking in the brilliant nectar flowing from his lotus feet...

All those praised by the gods—Brahmā and the rest—laugh at the wonderful nectar consisting of the bliss of divine love; they do not hold the great Vaiṣṇavas in high esteem, and they revile those learned in knowledge and ritual action. We praise that Gaura alone. 99 (6)

That path which is difficult to traverse and void, which here indeed has the thorns of the senses, which is exceedingly hard to reach and deludes one with false objects, yet which instantly pours forth the outflow of the bliss of aesthetic rasa—
that [path], its greatness revealed, suddenly illuminates it within the cave of the heart as if with affection.
Victorious is that destroyer of inner darkness, the shining lamp of Navadvīpa!
From afar he burns away the moths of fallacious reasoning; his sweetness is intensified by the union of the radiant light of ten million moons, and he removes the darkness both within and without.
With a disposition and activity full of affection, his divine splendor radiating forth, he possesses a golden luster;
out of compassion, that wondrous lamp of Navadvīpa blazes here.
(101) It is there that the Lord himself, fair as molten gold, dwells out of compassion.
A form consisting of the essence of the radiant nectar of the bliss of great love appeared;
my mind delights in that Navadvīpa, which is filled with the festival of devotion to the Lord and is a realm more sweet than even Vaikuṇṭha. (102) (62)
Bearing an indescribable complexion with the essence of gold as if emerged from fire,
assuming some divine form belonging to the proud Lord of the Gopas,
and manifesting various wondrous pastimes on certain occasions—
The fair-complexioned moon shines as the very personification of Rādhā and Madhuripu.
(103) Let the scriptures say what they will, and let the logicians explain as they may;
my life's sustenance is indeed the nectar of Caitanya’s lotus feet. (104)

Making the quarters of the sky resonant with the sounds of his foot-strikes, muddying the earth with streams of tears from his eyes, and oh, illuminating the heavens with his loud, boisterous laughter;
he whose crimson garment flutters about his noble and beautiful hips, which are as radiant as the moonlight.
"Which god dances with joy in the flower garden on the shore of the salt ocean? (105) (136) "Fie upon this illustrious lineage! Fie upon eloquence! Fie upon fame!
Fie upon learning, and fie as well upon my physical form, my youthful vigor, and my beauty!"
Fie upon the status of the twice-born, and fie upon the first stage of life if it is not pure, provided that the Lord of the fair-complexioned gopīs is not known in this Kali age! (106) (43)
Many dwell in mountain caves meditating and experiencing Brahman;
many on this earth are perfected ones devoted to the practice of yoga;
and many, falsely arrogant due to their learning, valor, wealth, and so forth, prance about.
Who else in this world, apart from Gaurī’s grace, could dance today, intoxicated with love? (107) (98) She who forcibly uproots the mass of inner darkness for all worlds,
and who powerfully causes the boundless ocean of the nectar of the bliss of love to surge forth.

May that radiance of the moon of consciousness, which incessantly cools the universe that is utterly distressed by the three-fold heat, shine forever within our hearts. (108) Or rather, let millions of excellent gurus be worshipped.
Or let them study millions of scriptures and treatises;
for those who receive the side-glance of Consciousness and Compassion, the supreme attainment of the secret occurs instantly. (109) (25)
Indeed, the feet of Caitanya, worshipped by Brahmā and Śiva, are the treasury of the boundless ocean of the nectar of the secret essence of the radiant rasa of divine love;
therefore, let them meditate upon Him and go for refuge with a weight of affection.
Let only those who are mad [with devotion] and those who are truly accomplished sing of that very thing here;

for therein lies the supreme purport of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, as delineated by the venerable son of Vyāsa, which—due to its profound and difficult connection—is found even within the context of the Rāsa-līlā. //110(89)//
Hari has descended into the world in a fair-complexioned body to manifest that Reality which is the sole true vessel for tasting the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the amorous play of Rādhā’s delight;
he does not discriminate between worthy and unworthy recipients, nor does he distinguish between himself and others. (111) (122)
The Lord does not deliberate over what should or should not be given, nor does He wait for the right time;
He who immediately bestows the rare essence of devotion through hearing, seeing, bowing, meditating, and so forth—that very same golden-hued Blessed One is my supreme refuge. (112) (77)

Some, headed by Uddhava, attained a praiseworthy state of servitude; others obtained the positions of Śrīdāmā and the rest among the lotus-eyed women of Vraja; still others embraced the ecstatic mood (bhāva) of those women;
while others, most fortunate of all, drink from the sweet ocean of the nectar of Rādhā.
By the mercy of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, what riches has the world not obtained?

(113) (123) Previously, when the various systems were extensively propagated by the all-knowing, preeminent sages through their respective reasonings, there was no person who placed firm confidence in any one of them alone.
Now that the moon-like fair-complexioned Lord has risen with incomparable splendor, who indeed would not determine that the supreme meaning of the Vedas is devotion to Hari alone?
(114) I have been deceived, I have been deceived, I have been deceived—of this there is no doubt! (124)

The entire universe was immersed in the nectar of the fair-complexioned Lord, so that even my sense of touch ceased to exist. (115) Oh, even by the excellent attendants of the Blessed One residing in Vaikuṇṭha,
the faces of the Lord's servants, headed by Mukhānucara and Iśvara, were seen with their hair standing on end!

How could one who has not performed meritorious deeds worship that fair-complexioned Lord, whose limbs are rendered helpless by the constant possession of the nectar of a most wonderful and radiant love?
Or by whom can this crest-jewel of all human goals be attained here without effort? (44) 116.
On this circle of the earth touched by the dust of the lotus feet of Gaurī, alas, alas!
Fie upon my life, fie upon my learning, and fie upon my stage of life, since—oh, what a burden of misfortune!—not even a trace of connection with Him has occurred for me. (117) (47)
[He] who completely submerges the entire universe in the singular ocean of the nectar-essence of the wine of great passion—
the radiance of the moonstone-like nails of the fair-limbed moon.
I remember a certain wondrous power:
even today, by the power of recollecting Gaurī, victory has been won again and again;
the wildernesses of evil doctrines have been crossed, and all my heart's desires are fulfilled.

Placing a blade of grass between my teeth, falling at your feet, and uttering a hundred plaintive cries, I say this: O virtuous ones, having abandoned everything from afar, [why do you not take me with you?]
Cultivate devotion at the feet of the moon-like Gaurāṅga! (120) (90) Even if rare accomplishments fall into the palm of one's hand of their own accord,
and even if the gods themselves should come to become one's servants;
What else could it be? Even if this body of mine were to become four-armed, my mind would not waver even slightly from Gaura-candra.
Oh, liberation is not difficult to attain, nor is devotion exceedingly rare!

But the grace of Gauracandra is exceedingly difficult to obtain even in Vaikuṇṭha. That Lord is composed of wonders; that which was not within the range of my eyes, and that taste of the lotus feet of Hari which was not savored—that which has passed away is truly gone. (122) (91)
Let this much suffice for me: that there be a festival of association with those whose minds are firmly planted at the feet of Śrī Caitanya, who even today continue to adorn the world.
(123) [The sound] surged forth, filling the entire universe.
Gauracandra is a great ocean of compassion; that not even a single drop has fallen upon me, so ill-fated—what a wonder this is! 124 (48)
The age is Kali; the hosts of enemies that are the senses are powerful; here, the path of glorious devotion is obstructed by millions of thorns!
Alas, alas! Where shall I go, being so distressed? What can I do?
O Caitanya-candra, if you do not show mercy today—
having abandoned the shimmering, magnificent Vṛndāvana on the banks of the Yamunā, you have gone to the flower-garden on the shore of the salt ocean.
Clad in saffron robes, having cast aside his bright yellow garment, Hari—whose own natural luster is concealed and whose fair radiance is now manifest—is my refuge.
(126) Let there be the pinnacle of dispassion; let there be the pinnacle of tranquility, self-restraint, forbearance, loving-kindness, and so forth.
Whether it be the pinnacle of meditation on reality or the pinnacle of devotion to Viṣṇu,

not even a ten-millionth part of these would equal the multitude of virtues that exist by their own nature among those who partake in the fragrance of the light from the toenails of the beloved feet of the glorious Moon-like Caitanya. (127) (26)
May they worship the lotus feet of Caitanya,
may they become filled with the nectar of true devotion,
and may they bring joy to the three worlds with their manifold [virtues].
By means of sweetness, charm, compassion, forbearance, and so forth,
may they accomplish knowledge, dispassion, devotion, and the like, in whatever way possible. //128(92)//
Where else can there be anything equal to that which is obtainable through devotion to the lotus feet of Caitanya?
Alas, alas! On the soil of a mind that is utterly barren... (129) (94)
Even millions of my spiritual practices become futile;
therefore, with my whole being, I take refuge in the feet of Śrī Gauracandra, that wondrous seed of devotion. (130) (52)
Even one devoid of all means of accomplishment, if their devotion is fixed upon the fair-limbed Lord of supreme and wondrous majesty, is indeed fulfilled in every aim.
(131) Even the Great Lord, whose greatness is a source of wonder for Brahmā, Śiva, and others—
Having heard what was spoken by an innocent child, he will surely become affectionate.
(132) (142) This has not been seen in the scriptures, nor have the teachers been consulted, nor has it been discerned by the wise through their own intellect.
However he may prattle due to his childish nature, may Gaurahari nevertheless be gracious to me. (133) (143) Some indeed exert their prowess even against the oceans and mountains; they truly dance.
Some, such as Deva, Purandara, and others, repeatedly hurl great insults;
yet who are these Advaityas, Candras, and the like, overwhelmed by the mass of their own arrogant joy?
What indeed could they possibly do against us during such a festival of Caitanya’s dancing? (134) (27)
When Gauracandra has descended and the ocean of love has expanded,
those who do not immerse themselves therein immerse themselves instead in the ocean of great misfortune.
(135) [In this] ocean of the nectar-essence of outstretched, great love...
When the moon of consciousness has appeared, he who is wretched remains truly wretched.
(136) Let him read the Gītā and the Bhāgavata incessantly; let him serve the holy pilgrimage sites or worship the Śālagrāma stone three times every day.

Without the compassion for the pair of feet of the Son of Śacī— that devotion consisting of pure love which acts as the sprout of the ornaments within His treasury— a person does not obtain that which is greater than all forms of liberation.
(137) He whose hope is fixed upon the pair of feet of the Great Lord Caitanya...
Even Indra appears like a mere servant to him; what need be said, then, of a worm among kings?
(138) For one whose hope is fixed on Kṛṣṇacaitanya, what purpose is there in the gates of a king?
Having obtained a heap of wish-fulfilling gems, who would go about in secret seeking common silver? (139)
He whose roar is the *huṃ* of ten million intoxicated lion-kings, whose splendor is like ten million suns,
who is as cool as ten million moons, and who has surpassed ten million rutting elephants with his gait;
he who by name effects the atonement for ten million misdeeds, the Lord of Brahmā and ten million others.
Victorious is the son of Śrī Śacī, the crest-jewel of non-dualism beyond all millions.

(140) (103) By some extraordinary ancestors, through supreme merit and great virtuous deeds, a certain purpose was fulfilled: that which no others have ever done—immersing the entire universe in an ocean of love. (141) (126)
Even if Gauracandra were not like the aforementioned portions beginning with the Fish (Mīna), he would nonetheless be a certain manifestation of the expansion of power and play,
through the manifestations of incomparable and wondrous pastimes of his entire potency.
One who has not yet attained greatness descends [into this path] already full. (142) (141) If there were a heart intent on crossing the ocean of saṃsāra,
and if the mind delights in the nectar-like flavor of kīrtana;
If the mental faculty is inclined toward sporting in the ocean of love, let it seek refuge at the feet of the Moon of Consciousness.
(143) [For] this universe is insentient; if the Lord were not consciousness, [it would remain so].
Death should be worshipped from all sides by those who are the best among the immortals.
